ENT Clinical Note – Telehealth Consult

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • Two-day history of progressive wheeze and shortness of breath after cleaning dusty carpet at home (suspected dust exposure).
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset ~1 hour after dust exposure two days ago. 
  • Gradual worsening, particularly at night. 
  • Currently limits ability to finish sentences during conversation.
- ENT symptoms:
  • No throat swelling/closure sensation.
  • No voice change/hoarseness.
  • No dysphagia, odynophagia, or drooling.
  • No nasal/ocular itching or rhinorrhea reported today (history of seasonal hay fever).
  • No stridor or noisy upper-airway breathing reported.
  • Dyspnea and wheeze present.
  • No facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling.
  • No ear pain/hearing change; no neck pain/swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Childhood asthma (intermittent; uses inhaler occasionally when running).
  • Seasonal hay fever; usually untreated with medication.
  • No prior hospitalizations or adrenaline injections for allergy/asthma reported.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug/food/environmental allergies: none known.
  • Medications on hand: Asthma inhaler (type/dose/route/frequency not documented); not used for current episode. No antihistamines at home.
- Social context:
  • Patient alone during call; GP surgery ~10 minutes’ drive away.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported or visualized.
- Airway/breathing: Patient verbally reports wheeze and shortness of breath; no stridor noted over video/audio.
- Mental status: Alert, oriented; denies dizziness or syncope.
- Vitals & physical examination: Not recorded.
- Companion: None present.

Assessment:
- Suspected asthma exacerbation vs. dust-induced allergic lower-airway reaction in patient with childhood asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis.
- Justification: Temporal relation to heavy dust exposure, progressive wheeze, history of asthma, absence of upper-airway swelling/throat symptoms.

Plan:
- Immediate actions/advice:
  • Obtain over-the-counter non-sedating antihistamine today and take per package instructions (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  • Proceed to in-person GP/clinic visit today for objective assessment: pulse oximetry, respiratory exam, and consideration of steroid therapy.
- Escalation criteria/red flags reviewed:
  • Call emergency services (999) or present to ED if any of the following occur: increased breathing difficulty, inability to speak in full sentences, chest tightness unrelieved by inhaler, audible wheeze at rest, stridor, throat tightness, facial or tongue swelling, or dizziness/syncope.
- Follow-up:
  • GP to receive letter summarizing telehealth encounter; anticipated face-to-face visit duration ≈10 minutes.
  • Discuss/update regular asthma management, inhaler technique, and consider allergy testing at follow-up.
  • Reinforce avoidance of heavy dust exposure and advise mask use during cleaning.
- Emergency contact instruction:
  • “Call 999” if breathing worsens or red flags develop (as stated above).

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing but clinically expected data: objective vitals (HR, RR, BP, SpO₂), chest/airway exam, peak-flow measurement, inhaler type and dosing, detailed medication list, prior exacerbation history, availability of rescue bronchodilator.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional brief drop in video but no loss of clinical information.
